Lizard · Introduced · Seen year-round

Brown Anole

Anolis sagrei
Perched on the hand-painted sign for the native plant garden. Brown anoles are from Cuba.
On this page

At a glance

  • If you see a small brown lizard doing push-ups on a fence post or flashing a reddish-orange throat fan, that is a brown anole — almost certainly the most common lizard you will meet anywhere in Florida.
  • It is not from here. Brown anoles arrived from Cuba and the Bahamas in the late 1800s and have since spread into nearly every county in the state.
  • Their success came at a cost to Florida's native green anole, which now spends more time high in the trees to stay out of the newcomer's way.
  • Males stake out territory with a stretchy throat flap called a dewlap and a bobbing push-up display — body language that says this spot is taken.

How to know it

Easily confused with

Green Anole — The green anole can turn bright green and has a pink throat fan and climbs higher; the brown anole never turns green, flashes a reddish-orange fan, and stays low.

Color

Shades of brown, tan, or gray, often with a pattern of triangles, diamonds, or a light stripe down the back. Unlike the green anole, it cannot turn green.

Throat fan (dewlap)

Males flash a reddish-orange dewlap edged in yellow during displays.

Body

Stocky, with a fairly short pointed snout and ridged (keeled) scales that give the back a slightly rough look.

Behavior cue

Usually seen low down — on the ground, fences, walls, and the base of trees — doing push-up displays.

Voice

Essentially silent. Anoles communicate with body language — push-ups and the colorful dewlap — rather than sound.

Size

5 to 8 inches, including the tail; males are larger than females.

What to look for

A small brown lizard perched head-down on a post or trunk, bobbing up and down. If it flashes an orange throat fan, it is a displaying male. The one thing it will never do is turn bright green — that is the native green anole, which tends to stay higher up.

Where to find it here

Almost everywhere on warm days — fence rails, tree trunks, sidewalk edges, and sunny garden borders. Watch low surfaces for a brown lizard doing push-ups.

Year-round resident. Most active and visible on warm, sunny days; scarce during cold snaps.

When

Most active on warm, sunny days; scarce in cold snaps.

How it lives

Active by day and almost always low to the ground. Males are territorial and constantly signal with head-bobbing push-ups and dewlap flashes. When threatened, an anole can drop its tail to escape a predator, then slowly regrow it. They bask to warm up and are most visible on warm, sunny days.

Insects and other small invertebrates — beetles, ants, flies, spiders, and just about anything it can catch and fit in its mouth. It will also eat the eggs and young of other lizards, including the native green anole.

What it does here

Native to Cuba, the Bahamas, and nearby Caribbean islands. Brown anoles first turned up in the Florida Keys around 1887, likely hitching rides in cargo and on nursery plants, and have spread through nearly the entire state. Today they are considered one of Florida's most abundant land vertebrates.

A major link in the local food chain. Brown anoles eat enormous numbers of insects and are in turn eaten by birds, snakes, larger lizards, and cats. Their sheer abundance makes them an important food source, but that same abundance is what pressures the native green anole.

Introduced and invasive in Florida. Native to Cuba and the Bahamas, established in the state since the late 1800s, and now one of its most abundant lizards. Its spread is linked to the decline of the native green anole through competition and predation on green anole young.

The brown anole's arrival reshaped life for Florida's only native anole, the green anole. The two lizards want the same things — similar food, similar perches, similar sunny spots — so where browns move in, greens tend to move higher, shifting up into shrubs and trees. Brown anoles will also eat green anole hatchlings and eggs, which adds to the pressure.

There is a fascinating wrinkle to the story. Scientists have watched green anoles evolve larger, stickier toepads over just a few generations — an adaptation that helps them grip the higher, smoother perches they have been pushed onto. It is one of the clearest real-world examples of rapid evolution happening right under our noses.

The brown anole isn't doing anything wrong; it is simply very good at being a lizard in Florida. But its quiet, ongoing story is a nice reminder of how an introduced species can reshape life for the natives already here — unfolding right in our own garden beds.
